claim: On 18 JUN 2023 about 10:47 a.m. local time, diving to the Titanic wreck about 370 nautical miles southeast of St. John's, Titan's pressure hull failed and it imploded; all five aboard died
source_quote: On June 18, 2023, about 1047 local time, while diving to the wreck of the ocean liner Titanic in the North Atlantic Ocean, about 372 miles southeast of St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, the submersible Titan’s pressure hull failed, and the vessel imploded. All five persons on board the vessel died.
note: PDF p. 7. Distance: exec summary says 372, abstract and 2.1 say 370 (nautical miles); say 'about 370 nautical miles'

claim: The USCG Marine Board of Investigation called the deaths a preventable tragedy
source_quote: Five people died when the commercial submersible TITAN imploded on June 18, 2023, in what is considered to be a preventable tragedy.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 5. Attribute: the board's word

claim: The pressure hull was a carbon-fibre composite cylinder of five 1-inch-thick co-bonded layers, with titanium rings glued on and titanium domes bolted to them
source_quote: two delaminations between the five 1-inch-thick layers that comprised the vessel’s carbon fiber composite cylinder | The titanium segments were glued to the cylinder, and the titanium domes were bolted to the segments.
note: PDF pp. 59, 8

claim: The Titanic wreck lies at 3,840 m (12,730 ft per NTSB 1.1.2; 12,598 ft in the dive-depth lines)
source_quote: at a depth of 3,880 meters (12,730 feet) | the 3,840-meter (12,598-foot) dive depth required to reach the Titanic
note: CONFLICT inside the NTSB report: wreck depth 3,880 m (PDF p. 8) vs dive depth to reach it 3,840 m (PDF p. 58). Use 'the dives reached 3,840 m' only; never give the wreck depth until settled

claim: OceanGate's original design goal was 6,000 m with a 2.25 safety factor and a 10,000-dive life
source_quote: The company’s original optimal design goal was for the submersible to be rated to dive up to 6,000 meters (19,680 feet) with a 2.25 safety factor and a 10,000-cycle life limit.
note: PDF p. 24

claim: The final hull was pressure-tested to about 4,200 m (6,154 psi), held for one 20-minute cycle, on 01 MAR 2021, at the Deep Ocean Test Facility in Bethesda, Maryland
source_quote: On March 1, 2021, the second DOTF test began at 6:53 a.m. and was completed at 5:40 p.m. The TITAN was tested to a maximum depth of approximately 4,200 m (6,154 psi) and it was held at that maximum pressure for one 20-minute cycle.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 184 (4.28.3). NTSB PDF p. 58: 'marginally greater than the 3,840-meter (12,598-foot) dive depth required to reach the Titanic'

claim: Two later DOTF runs held 3,840 m (about 5,627-5,628 psi) for 240 minutes each, 02 and 03 MAR 2021
source_quote: The TITAN was tested to a maximum depth of approximately 3,840 m (5,627 psi) and it was held at that maximum pressure for one 240-minute cycle.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 185

claim: Dive 80, 15 JUL 2022, at 3:26:45 p.m. the hull monitor recorded a major acoustic event (AE channel 2 peak 25,687 mV) and strain group 4 jumped: hoop +15.62 mV, longitudinal -30.5 mV
source_quote: At 3:26:45 p.m., the TITAN’s RTM system recorded a major acoustic emission event that included the following significant readings: AE Channel 2 peaked at 25,687 mV | The TITAN’s hoop strain (green line, labeled “R” in Figure 261), increased by 15.62 mV. The longitudinal strain (purple line, labeled “A”) decreased by 30.5 mV.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF pp. 283-284. Note 3:26:45 (event) vs 3:26:56 (delamination, same section); check the docket before choosing

claim: AE channels 1, 3 and 5 were inoperable for the whole 2022 expedition
source_quote: Channels 1, 3, and 5 are shown in red because they were confirmed by the MBI to be inoperable for the entire 2022 TITANIC Expedition and most likely remained inoperable for the duration of the 2023 Expedition.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 282-283

claim: The NTSB found the hull likely sustained damage (one or more delaminations) after it surfaced at the end of dive 80
source_quote: We found that the Titan pressure vessel likely sustained damage after it surfaced at the end of dive 80 in the form of one or more delaminations, which weakened the pressure vessel.
note: PDF p. 7

claim: Before dive 80 the hull's strain response was linear; after it, some gauges turned non-linear near the surface (dives 81-83), consistent with delamination
source_quote: While the strain response on dives leading up to dive 80, when the loud bang occurred, were linear, the strain response on dives after that event were non-linear for some strain gages when the vessel was near the surface.
note: PDF pp. 58-59; the hero exhibit

claim: The NTSB found OceanGate's analysis of the monitoring data flawed, so it did not know the Titan was damaged and needed immediate removal from service after dive 80
source_quote: OceanGate’s analysis of Titan pressure vessel real-time monitoring data was flawed, so the company was unaware that the Titan was damaged and needed to be immediately removed from service after dive 80.
note: PDF p. 7

claim: Phil Brooks (engineering director from 2021) testified that after dive 80 he discussed the strain shift with Rush, who 'wanted to continue on', and 'I think the plan was at that time to "well, let's dive again and see what happens" on 81'
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: I know I discussed it with Stockton and he -- you know, he wanted to continue on, that I think the plan was at that time to "well, let's dive again and see what happens" on 81, on the next dives
note: CG 112 transcript p. 764 of 1651 (Brooks, sworn). Quote with 'I think the plan was'; NTSB PDF p. 36 gives it as the CEO's words to the director of engineering

claim: After dive 80 OceanGate assessed the outside only; the insert was never removed to examine the inner carbon-fibre layer; it concluded the hull had shifted in its frame
source_quote: OceanGate performed a post-dive external assessment of the TITAN due to the loud bang. However, the TITAN’s insert was never removed to examine the structural integrity of the hull’s interior carbon fiber layer.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 233 (4.34.8.2)

claim: After dive 80, Titan dived twice more to 3,840 m (dives 81, 82) and once to 2,954 m (dive 83) in July 2022
source_quote: The Titan completed three additional dives following dive 80 (mission 4, dives 81-83); the submersible reached 3,840 meters (12,598 feet) on dives 81 and 82 and 2,954 meters (9,692 feet) on the final dive of the expedition.
note: PDF p. 36

claim: Dive 83 date
source_quote: 83 7/23/2022 2,954 Exploration | During dive 83 (July 25, 2022), the final successful dive
note: Appendix C (PDF p. 79) says 23 JUL; the analysis (PDF p. 59) says 25 JUL. Do not state the date

claim: In 2023, dives 84-87 reached 8-10 m only; dive 88 on 18 JUN 2023 was the first deep dive since July 2022
source_quote: 84 5/22/2023 8 Disabled sub drill | 85 5/31/2023 10 Test | 86 6/5/2023 10 Test | 87 6/12/2023 10 Aborted dive | 88 6/18/2023 3,363 (last known depth) Casualty dive
note: Appendix C, PDF pp. 79-80. 'First deep dive in eleven months' is our reading of the table; say it as the dive log

claim: On 28 JUL 2022 the storage yard quoted $1,750 for a protective cover; OceanGate's Director of Integration and Operations reportedly did not respond
source_quote: On July 28, 2022, a quote was provided by A Harvey for a protective cover for the TITAN at a cost of $1,750, but OceanGate’s Director of Integration and Operations reportedly did not respond to the email proposal.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 322 (5.20). 'reportedly' stays

claim: Titan stayed uncovered in the parking lot until 06 FEB 2023, through temperatures from 1.4°F to 84.2°F
source_quote: the TITAN continued to remain uncovered in the same exposed location at the A Harvey Marine Base until February 6, 2023 | temperatures ranging from 1.4° F to 84.2° F
note: PDF p. 322-323. SI on screen: -17°C to 29°C

claim: The USCG board found storage 'likely accelerated material degradation'; the NTSB calls the damage after dive 82 'of unknown origin'
source_quote: likely accelerated material degradation, including potential weakening of the hull and other critical components | additional damage (of unknown origin)
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); USCG PDF p. 324; NTSB PDF p. 7. Both said, side by side

claim: Rush left the Director of Engineering post vacant before the 2023 season (the USCG board's finding)
source_quote: To ensure the 2023 TITANIC Expedition proceeded unhindered, Mr. Rush left the Director of Engineering position vacant ahead of TITAN’s 2023 operations.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 320. The board's reading of motive: attribute

claim: The last Director of Engineering left in early 2023 because 'the safety was being compromised way too much'
source_quote: The Director of Engineering stated to the MBI he decided to leave OceanGate in early 2023 because “…the safety was being compromised way too much, at least for myself.”
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 319-320

claim: On 18 JAN 2018 the Director of Marine Operations submitted an inspection report listing 26 components needing corrective action
source_quote: on January 18, 2018, submitted a report highlighting critical safety concerns ... he outlined 26 components that required corrective action or further attention
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 146

claim: The USCG board cited financial pressures: employees asked to forgo salaries; Rush advanced the company $1.85M from June 2022 to May 2023
source_quote: From June 2022 to May 2023, Mr. Rush advanced OceanGate Inc. a total of $1.85 million.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 319

claim: The NTSB's probable cause: OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, which failed to establish the hull's actual strength and durability
source_quote: We determined that the probable cause of the hull failure and implosion of the submersible Titan was OceanGate’s inadequate engineering process, which failed to establish the actual strength and durability of the Titan pressure vessel
note: PDF p. 8

claim: Titan imploded at about 3,363 m (11,032 ft) on dive 88
source_quote: at a depth about 11,032 feet (3,363 meters), the submersible Titan’s hull failed
note: PDF p. 58. NOTE: 2.2 gives '3,363 meters (10,032 feet)' on the same page: a typo in feet; use 11,032

claim: Titan reached the Titanic wreck site 13 times in 2021 and 2022
source_quote: During the 2021 and 2022 expeditions, the Titan successfully dove to the Titanic wreck site 13 times.
note: PDF p. 58

claim: Correction: no record supports 'expired carbon fibre'; the final hull's prepreg was bought from Toray (7,700 lbs, $332,101 PO, 21 FEB 2020)
source_quote: On February 21, 2020, OceanGate issued a purchase order for 7,700 lbs of P2362W-190U-013 composite material from Toray Composites, valued at $332,101.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 174. For a viewer question, not the script

claim: Horizon Arctic was unavailable for 2023; OceanGate used Polar Prince and towed Titan on its launch platform
source_quote: The HORIZON ARCTIC, which was utilized as the support vessel for Expeditions 2021 and 2022, was unavailable for use by OceanGate for 2023 operations.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/; text identical to the reading copy on all 335 pages, 13 NOV 2026); PDF p. 245. 5.20 calls it a 'decision': say 'unavailable' (the finding of fact)

claim: OceanGate analysed strain against time; the NTSB says the appropriate method was against depth (a stress/strain plot), and re-plotting it that way found the change after dive 80
source_quote: OceanGate analyzed data from the strain gages against time. However, analyzing strain data in this way was flawed because it was difficult for OceanGate to compare data between dives. A more appropriate means of evaluating strain data would have been to evaluate it against depth | after the implosion, the NTSB evaluated the Titan strain data against the vessel’s depth and identified the change in the low-depth strain response in the pressure vessel after dive 80.
note: PDF p. 64 (2.4). The signature build

claim: OceanGate based its acoustic evaluation on earlier hulls made by a different method; after dive 80 the sensors never produced the kind of signal that would have triggered an alert
source_quote: OceanGate based their evaluation of acoustic emission data on the signals from previous Titan pressure vessels—the v1 full-scale hull and sub-scale models. | The sensors produced activity on the dives that followed dive 80 but never produced the type of acoustic emission signal that would have triggered an alert and thus did not detect the initial damage.
note: PDF pp. 64-65

claim: OceanGate analysed acoustic data only during dives, so damage at the surface or in storage could not be captured
source_quote: OceanGate only analyzed acoustic emission data captured during a dive, so the data could not be used to capture and alert crew to damaging events that occurred at the surface or while the Titan was stowed.
note: PDF p. 64

claim: Asked who decided to resume diving after the bang, Brooks answered: 'Definitely Stockton.'
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: Q. So who made the decision to continue to resume diving operations after the report of the loud bang? A. Definitely Stockton.

claim: Brooks: the post-dive-80 inspection was mainly the strain and acoustic data, because the insert inside and the covering outside made the hull hard to inspect; the strain showed 'a shift in the level' on two of the 16 channels
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: we did an inspection of the hull as best we could, but it's hard because there's the insert on the inside and then, of course, it's covered on the outside. | the strain data does show a shift in the level | two of the strain channels, two out of the 16
note: CG 112 pp. 764-765. Brooks also cites a '5,000 threshold' for acoustic activity: unit unclear, LEAD ONLY, never compared with 25,687 mV

claim: Brooks left in early 2023 and testified the safety was 'being compromised way too much. At least for myself.'
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: being compromised way too much. At least for myself.
note: CG 112 (Brooks); also USCG ROI PDF pp. 319-320 (C22)

claim: The RTM system had eight acoustic emission sensors, eight hoop and eight longitudinal strain gauges
source_quote: The system was comprised of eight acoustic emission sensors, eight circumferential (hoop) strain gages, and eight longitudinal (axial) strain gages.
note: NTSB 1.3.4

claim: 18 JUN 2023: Titan released about 9:00 a.m.; the first 2023 dive below 33 ft (10 m); at 10:47 a.m., at 3,363 m, it messaged it was dropping two weights; no reply after that
source_quote: About 0900, the Titan was released from the LARS and began its descent | It was the first dive of the 2023 expedition to descend below 33 feet (10 meters). | At 1047, while the Titan was at a depth of 11,032 feet (3,363 meters), OceanGate received a message that the submersible was dropping two weights | At 1048, the Polar Prince sent a message back to acknowledge the Titan’s message, but they received no response.
note: NTSB 1.1.3

claim: On 22 JUN 2023 at 9:40 a.m. the ROV Odysseus found the debris field, including the tail cone and both titanium domes, about 500 m from the Titanic's bow
source_quote: At 0940, the Odysseus discovered a debris field consistent with the Titan, including the tail cone and both titanium domes, near the submersible’s last known position, about 500 meters (1,148 feet) northeast of the bow of the Titanic.
note: NTSB 1.2

claim: The USCG board: had Rush survived it would have recommended the Commandant refer the matter to the DoJ; whether any crime was committed would be the DoJ's determination, which will not occur
source_quote: Had OceanGate’s CEO and chief pilot survived the incident, the MBI would have recommended that the Commandant refer the matter to DoJ for their consideration on whether to pursue a separate criminal investigation. | It is important to note that the determination of whether any crime was committed would be made by the DoJ following its own investigation and analysis, which will not occur in this instance due to the death of Mr. Rush.
note: USCG ROI 6.5, PDF p. 330. Say both sentences together, always

claim: After communications were lost, 'this was not perceived to be an emergency by OceanGate' (the Polar Prince captain)
source_quote: According to the Polar Prince captain, “this was not perceived to be an emergency by OceanGate.”
note: NTSB 1.1.3; attributed to the captain

claim: NTSB least-squares slope of depth vs strain (15-150 m), group 4 hoop gauge: dives 75 and 80, 5.00 and 4.74 m/mV; after the event, dives 81, 82, 83: 8.76, 8.09, 8.77 m/mV
source_quote: The slopes for Dives 75 and 80, prior to the event, were 5.00 m/mV and 4.74 m/mV, respectively. After the event, the slopes for Dives 81, 82, and 83 were 8.76 m/mV, 8.09 m/mV, and 8.77 m/mV, respectively.
note: NTSB Materials Laboratory Factual Report 24-012 (D. Kramer), pp. 6-7; figs. 28-31 for the re-plot

claim: When the dive 80 bang occurred relative to the surface
source_quote: Shortly after surfacing, an audible “loud bang” was heard, according to the dive log. | (NTSB MIR-25-36 p. 30) heard a “loud bang” as the Titan ascended | (USCG ROI 5.7) The audible event occurred as the TITAN was still submerged and approaching the surface.
note: Three records differ: Materials report 'shortly after surfacing'; NTSB final 'as the Titan ascended'; USCG 'still submerged and approaching the surface'. Narration says 'near the surface' only

claim: In 2023 the towed Titan and its launch platform had multiple tipping/upset events before the first attempted dive; one damaged the tail cone
source_quote: The Titan and LARS experienced multiple tipping/upset events during the 2023 expedition leading up to the first attempted dive. | The bow of the LARS had tipped downward, causing damage to the tail cone
note: Materials report 24-012 p. 7-8, figs. 40a-c (rights check)

claim: The 18 JAN 2018 inspection report (first hull) cited visible delamination in the hull's machined-off end sections and warned of 'potential inter-laminar fatigue due to pressure cycling', recommending full non-destructive inspection
source_quote: As we have all seen the Carbon hull end sections that were machined off after the completion of the winding show very visible signs of delamination | we run the risk of potential inter-­laminar fatigue due to pressure cycling, this especially if we do have imperfections in the hull itself. | We should fully endorse what the company initially set out to do and carry out a full Non Destructive Inspection of both the hull and also the Bond line
note: USCG exhibit CG-098 (NTSB docket). FIRST hull (v1), not the hull lost in 2023: say so in the same sentence. Rights: OceanGate document in a federal docket; check before showing the scan

claim: The v2 stress analysis predicted a cylinder implosion depth of about 7,500 m; it limited Titan to 4,200 m because of possible deformation of the titanium forward dome around the viewport
source_quote: The second stress analysis predicted an implosion depth for the carbon fiber cylinder of about 7,500 meters (24,606 feet). It also indicated that the depth of the Titan was limited to 4,200 meters (13,790 feet) due to the potential for deformation of the titanium forward dome around the viewport.
note: NTSB PDF p. 27. So 4,200 m was a dome limit, not a measured cylinder strength

claim: The v2-method sub-scale models imploded or nearly imploded shallower than 3,000 m; the co-bonded design was never built as a test article: the only one was the hull that dived
source_quote: either imploded or nearly imploded at depths less than 3,000 meters (9,843 feet), significantly less than the depth needed to reach the Titanic wreckage | the only article produced using the co-bonding process was the v2 full-scale cylinder ultimately used in the casualty dive.
note: NTSB PDF p. 62

claim: OceanGate never tested a co-bonded hull to failure; the NTSB found it unlikely the built hull had the strength OceanGate's analysis predicted
source_quote: OceanGate never tested a co-bonded composite pressure hull to failure (full-scale or sub-scale) and, as a result, never established the strength or failure mode of that design. | it is unlikely that the fabricated hull would have had the strength predicted by OceanGate’s analysis.
note: NTSB PDF p. 63

claim: The NTSB: at greater depths the strain response stayed linear, indicating the gauges themselves had not changed but the hull had
source_quote: The strain response at greater depths remained linear, similar to previous dives, indicating that the gages themselves had not changed, but rather the pressure hull itself had changed.
note: NTSB PDF p. 59 (footnote 42). Answers 'sensor fault?'

claim: Dropping two weights at that depth was standard procedure to slow the descent
source_quote: OceanGate received a message that the submersible was dropping two weights (which was a standard procedure at this depth to slow its descent).
note: NTSB 1.1.3. Never imply the crew knew

claim: Dive 88 start and last-message depth differ between the reports
source_quote: About 0900, the Titan was released from the LARS | At 1047, while the Titan was at a depth of 11,032 feet (3,363 meters) || (USCG ROI) At approximately 9:14 a.m., the dive commenced | At 10:47:02 a.m., at a depth of 3,341 meters, the TITAN messaged
note: NTSB 9:00 / 3,363 m vs USCG 9:14 / 3,341 m. Say 'about 3,350 metres (records differ by 22 m)' or attribute each

claim: After a later debrief, per a contractor's testimony, Rush said the bang was probably the sled banging against the frame
source_quote: He said it was probably just the sled banging against the frame and then, oh well, deep-sea vehicles just make lots of noise due to pressure changes.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file); PDF p. 234. Testimony of one contractor: attribute. Do NOT use her account of the Director of Administration (refuted, footnote 46)

claim: The five who died: Stockton Rush (61, US, pilot and CEO), Paul-Henri Nargeolet (77, France), Shahzada Dawood (48, UK and Pakistan), Suleman Dawood (19, UK and Pakistan), Hamish Harding (58, UK)
source_quote: Richard Stockton Rush III ... 61 U.S. | Paul-Henri Nargeolet Content Expert Male 77 France | Shahzada Dawood Passenger/Mission Specialist #1 Male 48 U.K. and Pakistan | Suleman Dawood Passenger/Mission Specialist #2 Male 19 U.K. and Pakistan | Hamish Harding Passenger/Mission Specialist #3 Male 58 U.K.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file); Table 2, section 3

claim: The USCG board found OceanGate described paying passengers as 'mission specialists' with mandatory duties
source_quote: The operations and obligations of mission specialists participating in OceanGate's TITANIC expeditions were misrepresented by OceanGate as mandatory duties to conceal that their mission specialists were actually paying passengers.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file); PDF p. 317 (5.18). The board's finding: attribute

claim: Plots of strain and acoustic data as a function of time were prepared by OceanGate after each dive (the NTSB Materials report)
source_quote: were processed by OceanGate personnel after the dive, which was their typical procedure. Plots for acoustic activity and strain as a function of time for Dive 80, prepared by OceanGate
